cards.prompt: Select the revenue column from df as a Series.
cards.why: Bracket access with a single column name always returns a 1D Series, sharing df's index.
cards.whenToUse: You need the values of one column, e.g. to compute a sum or feed into a chart.
cards.commonMistake: Using df.revenue (dot access) — it works until the column name collides with a DataFrame method or has a space, then it silently breaks.

cards.prompt: Select the region and revenue columns together, keeping the result a DataFrame.
cards.why: A list of column names inside the brackets returns a DataFrame, even if the list has only one name.
cards.whenToUse: You need more than one column, or want to guarantee a DataFrame (not a Series) even for a single column.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting the inner brackets — df['region', 'revenue'] (no inner list) raises a KeyError.

cards.prompt: Add a new column revenue_per_unit computed from revenue divided by units.
cards.why: Assigning to a bracketed column name that doesn't exist yet creates it — pandas does the division element-wise across every row.
cards.whenToUse: Deriving a new column from one or more existing columns.
cards.commonMistake: Doing this on a DataFrame that's actually a filtered view/copy of another — pandas may raise a SettingWithCopyWarning.
cards.example: # adds a revenue_per_unit column, e.g. 10.0 for row 0

cards.prompt: Check the data type of just the revenue column.
cards.why: dtype (singular) is a Series attribute; dtypes (plural) is the DataFrame-level version covering every column at once.
cards.whenToUse: Confirming one specific column's type before doing arithmetic or comparisons on it.
cards.commonMistake: Writing df['revenue'].dtypes (plural) — it still works on a Series but is the wrong attribute name conceptually.

cards.prompt: Check how many dimensions df has.
cards.why: A DataFrame is always 2D (rows and columns); a Series is always 1D — ndim confirms which you're holding.
cards.whenToUse: Debugging when you're not sure whether a variable ended up as a Series or a DataFrame.
cards.commonMistake: Confusing ndim (dimension count) with shape (size along each dimension) — they answer different questions.

cards.prompt: Get the total number of elements in df (rows times columns).
cards.why: size multiplies rows by columns into a single number — shape gives you the two numbers separately.
cards.whenToUse: A rough sense of how much data you're holding, e.g. before an expensive operation.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting size to equal the row count (like len()) — it's rows * columns, not just rows.

cards.prompt: Make a full independent copy of df, so edits to the copy don't affect the original.
cards.why: Plain assignment (df2 = df) just creates a second name pointing at the same data — copy() actually duplicates it.
cards.whenToUse: Before making edits to a DataFrame you still need the original, unmodified version of.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming df2 = df is enough to protect df from later mutations to df2 — it isn't.
cards.example: # an identical DataFrame that no longer shares memory with df

cards.prompt: Convert df to a plain dict of lists, one list per column.
cards.why: to_dict() accepts an orient argument controlling the output shape — 'list' gives {column: [values...]}, the most common shape for exporting to plain Python.
cards.whenToUse: Handing DataFrame data off to code (or a JSON API) that only understands plain dicts/lists.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting the default orient is 'dict' (nested {column: {row_label: value}}), not the flatter 'list' shape.

cards.prompt: Convert df into a raw NumPy array, dropping the column labels and index. Fill in the blank.
cards.why: to_numpy() is the modern, explicit way to drop down to a plain array — the older .values attribute does the same thing but is less explicit about types with mixed columns.
cards.whenToUse: Feeding a DataFrame into a library (like NumPy or scikit-learn) that expects a plain array, not pandas objects.
cards.commonMistake: Forgetting that mixed dtypes (e.g. text and numbers together) force the whole array to a common dtype like object.

cards.prompt: Check whether 'revenue' is one of df's column names.
cards.why: in checks membership against the column Index directly — a quick guard before referencing a column that might not exist.
cards.whenToUse: Defensive checks before code that assumes a specific column is present, e.g. after a join or an external data load.
cards.commonMistake: Writing 'revenue' in df (without .columns) — that checks index labels for a Series, but for a DataFrame it happens to also check columns, which is easy to misremember and best avoided.

cards.prompt: Add a boolean column high_value that's True wherever revenue is over 100.
cards.why: A comparison against a column produces a boolean Series, which assigns cleanly as a new column, one True/False per row.
cards.whenToUse: Tagging rows with a derived flag you'll filter or group by later.
cards.commonMistake: Wrapping the comparison in df[...] first — that filters rows instead of producing a column to assign.
cards.example: # adds high_value: True for row 0 (120 > 100), False for row 1 (95 > 100)

cards.prompt: Transpose df, swapping rows and columns.
cards.why: T flips the DataFrame so former columns become the index and former rows become columns — mostly useful for small, wide summaries.
cards.whenToUse: A DataFrame with few rows and many columns (or vice versa) that would display or read better flipped.
cards.commonMistake: Transposing a large DataFrame with mixed dtypes — every value gets coerced to a common dtype (usually object), which can be surprising.
cards.example: # columns become row labels, row labels become column headers

cards.prompt: Get both of df's axes (its row index and its columns) in one call.
cards.why: axes returns a two-item list — [index, columns] — the same information index and columns give separately, bundled together.
cards.whenToUse: Code that needs to iterate over 'both axes' generically, without hardcoding which is which.
cards.commonMistake: Expecting axes[0] to be columns — it's [index, columns] in that order, index first.

cards.prompt: Randomly sample 2 rows from df, using a fixed random_state so the result is reproducible.
cards.why: sample() picks random rows rather than the first/last n like head()/tail() — random_state makes the 'random' choice reproducible across runs.
cards.whenToUse: Eyeballing a representative slice of a large DataFrame instead of just its beginning.
cards.commonMistake: Omitting random_state, so the sampled rows change every run — fine for exploration, unhelpful when trying to reproduce a bug.
cards.example: # 2 randomly chosen rows, exact ones fixed by random_state=0

cards.prompt: Which of these selects revenue and keeps the result a DataFrame, not a Series?
cards.why: A single name in single brackets (df['revenue']) or as an attribute (df.revenue) both return a Series; wrapping the name in a list forces a DataFrame.
cards.whenToUse: Any time downstream code (like a merge or a plot) requires a DataFrame, even for one column.
cards.commonMistake: Assuming df.revenue and df['revenue'] behave differently — they're equivalent, and both return a Series.
